---
title: "Probability Under Transformation"
---



Push a distribution through a function and it is **reshaped** — by the function's
derivative.  This is the same [change-of-variables](../gaussianization/01-change-of-variables.qmd)
rule that powers Gaussianization, now read as *uncertainty propagation*.

## The rule

For an invertible $y = f(x)$,

$$
p_Y(y) = p_X(x)\,\left|\frac{dx}{dy}\right| = \frac{p_X(x)}{\lvert f'(x)\rvert}.
$$

Where $f$ is **steep**, it spreads probability out (the output is more
uncertain); where it is **flat**, it concentrates it.  The Jacobian
$\lvert f'\rvert$ is the exact bookkeeping.

::: {#cell-fig-pushforward .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
f = lambda x: np.exp(0.55 * x)           # convex, option-like
x = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, 40000)
y = f(x)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 5.2))
# function curve
xs = np.linspace(-3, 3, 300)
ax.plot(xs, f(xs), c=INK, lw=2.2)
ax.set_xlabel("input x"); ax.set_ylabel("output y = f(x)")
# input density along the bottom
xb = np.linspace(-3, 3, 200)
ax.fill_between(xb, -0.3 + 2.0 * norm.pdf(xb), -0.3, color=COOL, alpha=0.5)
ax.text(-2.6, 0.5, "input p(x)", color=COOL, fontsize=10)
# output density along the left (rotated)
yb = np.linspace(y.min(), np.quantile(y, 0.999), 200)
hist, edges = np.histogram(y, bins=80, density=True)
cen = 0.5 * (edges[:-1] + edges[1:])
ax.fill_betweenx(cen, -3 + 2.5 * hist, -3, color=WARM, alpha=0.5)
ax.text(-2.9, np.quantile(y, 0.85), "output p(y)\n(skewed, heavy)",
        color=WARM, fontsize=10)
ax.set_xlim(-3, 3); ax.set_ylim(-0.4, np.quantile(y, 0.999))
ax.set_title("A distribution reshaped by its transform", fontsize=12)
despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![A Gaussian input pushed through a convex function. The output is skewed and stretched in the steep region — uncertainty is reshaped, not merely shifted.](02-probability-under-transformation_files/figure-html/fig-pushforward-output-1.png){#fig-pushforward width=884 height=609}
:::
:::


## Small-noise propagation

Linearize and the rule becomes the familiar engineering formula: a small input
noise $\sigma_x$ produces output noise

$$
\sigma_y \approx \lvert f'(x)\rvert\,\sigma_x.
$$

Error scales with the **slope of the system** — the steeper the response, the more
your input uncertainty is amplified.

::: {#cell-fig-error-propagation .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
f = lambda x: np.tanh(1.5 * x)
fp = lambda x: 1.5 * (1 - np.tanh(1.5 * x) ** 2)
xs = np.linspace(-2.5, 2.5, 300)
sig_x = 0.3
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.4))
ax.plot(xs, f(xs), c=INK, lw=2.2)
for x0, name in [(-0.1, "steep"), (1.6, "flat")]:
    sy = abs(fp(x0)) * sig_x
    ax.errorbar(x0, f(x0), yerr=sy, xerr=sig_x, fmt="o", color=CRASH,
                capsize=4, lw=2)
    ax.annotate(f"{name}: σ_y≈{sy:.2f}", (x0, f(x0)),
                textcoords="offset points", xytext=(10, -18), fontsize=10)
ax.set_xlabel("input x"); ax.set_ylabel("output f(x)")
ax.set_title("σ_y ≈ |f'(x)| · σ_x", fontsize=12)
despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Same input noise, two operating points. Where f is steep the output band is wide; where f is flat it is narrow.](02-probability-under-transformation_files/figure-html/fig-error-propagation-output-1.png){#fig-error-propagation width=885 height=513}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Why this matters for risk
Portfolio P&L is a *function* of returns.  Propagating return uncertainty to P&L
is exactly this push-forward — and because the function is multivariate, the
**joint** dependence of the inputs controls the joint tail of the output.  Keeping
that dependence is what the [next page](03-noise-and-propagation.qmd) is about.
:::
